comment:
The Guidance currently addresses national governance and then uses “regional governance” principally for multi-country arrangements, leaving an important governance model insufficiently covered: distribution of responsibilities within a country. 

Federal, devolved and decentralised health systems may combine shared national infrastructure with autonomous or subnational ownership and service-delivery responsibilities. 

This is not equivalent to undesirable fragmentation. For example: Spain provides an established implementation pattern: the Interterritorial Council created the Digital Health Commission specifically to support co-governance between the Ministry of Health and the Autonomous Communities and to ensure interoperability across public administrations. 

The national TSI/CIP-SNS (Tarjeta Sanitaria Individual / Código de identificación de paciente SNS) architecture similarly combines regional databases and management responsibilities with shared national identity and interoperability services. Explicitly addressing multi-level governance would improve the applicability of the Guidance to decentralised countries and would also reinforce the subsidiarity principle already included in Section 3.4.2

The Guidance currently addresses national governance and then uses “regional governance” principally for multi-country arrangements, leaving an important governance model insufficiently covered: distribution of responsibilities within a country. 

Federal, devolved and decentralised health systems may combine shared national infrastructure with autonomous or subnational ownership and service-delivery responsibilities.

public.suggestedRevision: Insert a new subsection immediately before the current Section 3.4.6: “Subnational and multi-level governance. In federal, devolved or otherwise decentralised health systems, legal responsibility, stewardship and operational control may be distributed between national and subnational public authorities. Governance should explicitly define: (i) decision rights at each level; (ii) common national or jurisdiction-wide interoperability and conformance requirements; (iii) capabilities and data remaining under subnational stewardship; (iv) co-governance, coordination and dispute-resolution mechanisms; and (v) accountability across federated nodes. A national DPI-H architecture does not require national ownership or operational control of all underlying systems or data.” Rename existing 3.4.6 “Cross-country and supranational governance considerations.”
